extracted.intended_audience: readers, writers, and students of literary criticism interested in comedy and the comic spirit
extracted.subtask_short: essay on comedy and comic perception
extracted.subtask_description: A literary-criticism lecture describing what the 'Comic' or comic spirit is, how it differs from satire, irony, and humour, and the qualities of comic writing and appreciation. Useful for readers and writers seeking principles for perceiving or composing comedy in literature and the theatre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting ridicule of those you love
rubrics_metrics.description: You may estimate your capacity for Comic perception by being able to detect the ridicule of them you love, without loving them less: and more by being able to see yourself somewhat ridiculous in dear eyes, and accepting the correction their image of you proposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is offered as a test of comic perception: the comic eye perceives flaws in intimates yet preserves affection. Example/implication: being able to laugh about quarrels with a partner rather than turning to bitter satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Satire from Comic perception
rubrics_metrics.description: If you detect the ridicule, and your kindliness is chilled by it, you are slipping into the grasp of Satire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satire is described as a moral agent, often a social scavenger, working on a storage of bile; it drives with sharp force and is a blow in the back or the face. Anti-pattern: letting moral heat and desire to wound replace the impersonal insight of the Comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Irony from Comic perception
rubrics_metrics.description: If instead of falling foul of the ridiculous person with a satiric rod, to make him writhe and shriek aloud, you prefer to sting him under a semi-caress, by which he shall in his anguish be rendered dubious whether indeed anything has hurt him, you are an engine of Irony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Irony is 'the humour of satire'; it may be savage (Swift) with moral object or sedate (Gibbon) with malice. Anti-patterns: foppish irony that frets to be seen or leering irony that reveals intention are failures in genuine ambiguity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing Humour from Comic perception
rubrics_metrics.description: If you laugh all round him, tumble him, roll him about, deal him a smack, and drop a tear on him, own his likeness to you and yours to your neighbour, spare him as little as you shun, pity him as much as you expose, it is a spirit of Humour that is moving you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour embraces contrasts, comforts, and sometimes allows feelings to overflow; great humour fuses tragic sentiment with the comic narrative (e.g., Don Quixote). Humourists may be sentimental or capricious when touching upon History or Society; they differ from the Comic in their emotional temper.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Comic (definition and boundaries)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic, which is the perceptive, is the governing spirit, awakening and giving aim to these powers of laughter, but it is not to be confounded with them: it enfolds a thinner form of them, differing from satire, in not sharply driving into the quivering sensibilities, and from humour, in not comforting them and tucking them up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Comic addresses the intellect, is impersonal and restrained, 'eyes but does not touch'—it perceives folly without cruelty. Anti-patterns: gross farce or derisive laughter that attacks misfortune (rather than exposed pretence) is 'too gross for Comedy.' Examples: Alceste and Tartuffe as purely comic figures addressed to intellect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim and scope of the Comic poet
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic poet is in the narrow field, or enclosed square, of the society he depicts; and he addresses the still narrower enclosure of men's intellects, with reference to the operation of the social world upon their characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He is concerned with 'what you are now weaving' — present social character and conduct, not with beginnings, endings, or extensive surroundings. To understand and value Comic work you must have a sober liking of your kind and a sober estimate of our civilized qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of true comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: One excellent test of the civilization of a country... I take to be the flourishing of the Comic idea and Comedy; and the test of true Comedy is that it shall awaken thoughtful laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True comedy produces reflective, intelligent amusement rather than merely noisy or brutish laughter. Example contrast: Aristophanes and Moliere (mindful laughter) versus passages of Rabelais or Peregrine Pickle (cataract of laughter but not illuminating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of comic laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughter of Comedy is impersonal and of unrivalled politeness, nearer a smile; often no more than a smile. It laughs through the mind, for the mind directs it; and it might be called the humour of the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contrasts with satire's blow and with coarse, noisy laughter. Comic laughter refines rather than humiliates; it indicates intellectual perception rather than mere derision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral limits of comic perception (what not to laugh at)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents of a kind casting ridicule on our unfortunate nature instead of our conventional life, provoke derisive laughter, which thwarts the Comic idea... Poverty is never ridiculous to Comic perception until it attempts to make its rags conceal its bareness in a forlorn attempt at decency, or foolishly to rival ostentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not direct derisive laughter at genuine misfortune; only the pretence or comic attempt to conceal misfortune invites comic perception. Anti-pattern: mistaking the poor themselves for comic subjects instead of the social pretence that makes them appear ridiculous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contrast as the vehicle of comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic spirit...refresh the intellect they quicken to detect their comedy, by force of the contrast they offer between themselves and the wiser world about them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy often arises from sharp contrasts between a character's self-image and the wiser or common-sense world; presenting such contrasts clearly quickens the reader's intellect and produces thoughtful laughter. Examples: Shakespeare, Cervantes, the juxtaposition of knight and squire in Don Quixote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint, measure, and taste in comic composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy, or in any form the Comic spirit, will then come to them to cut some figures out of the block... The French lay marked stress on 'mesure et gout', and they own how much they owe to Moliere for leading them in simple justness and taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comic writing requires a disciplined restraint and tasteful measure; avoid grossness and excess. The Moliere model: ethereal, measured comedy rather than noisy bawdy fun.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic poet's obligation to clarity and plan (advantage of stage writing)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a benefit to men in taking the lessons of Comedy in congregations, for it enlivens the wits; and to writers it is beneficial, for they must have a clear scheme... And writing for the stage would be a corrective of a too-incrusted scholarly style... It keeps minor writers to a definite plan, and to English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwriting discipline enforces a clear scheme, economy of expression, and accessibility. Advice for writers: stage-writing trains clarity and discourages over-ornate, pedantic prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader prerequisites: common-sense and civic sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: You must, as I have said, believe that our state of society is founded in common-sense, otherwise you will not be struck by the contrasts the Comic Spirit perceives... To understand his work and value it, you must have a sober liking of your kind and a sober estimate of our civilized qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers lacking faith in common-sense or civic sympathy may miss the Comic spirit and feel attacked or alienated by comic works. Cultivating polite society helps develop the inward eye that perceives comic contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic perception as civilizing influence
rubrics_metrics.description: A perception of the comic spirit gives high fellowship. You become a citizen of the selecter world... Good hope sustains you; weariness does not overwhelm you; in isolation you see no charms for vanity; personal pride is greatly moderated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay argues comedic sensibility benefits character and social life: it promotes humility, fellowship, and tempering of pride. This is presented as both personal and civic value of the Comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure modes: learned circles lacking Comic sense
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughter heard in circles not pervaded by the Comic idea, will sound harsh and soulless... They have in them, perhaps, every element composing light, except the Comic... Insufficiency of sight in the eye looking outward has deprived them of the eye that should look inward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: erudition, professorial arrogance, or purely scholarly circles may lack inward comic perception—leading to irritable personality and pugnacity. Remedy: practice in polite society or exposure to comic tradition.

rubrics_metrics.name: National/traditional cultivation affects comic faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the difference of traditions, temper, and style, which comes of schooling... The French controversialist is a polished swordsman... The Germans have gone through no comic training to warn them of the sly, wise emanation eyeing them from aloft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical and cultural schooling (Moliere, La Bruyere, La Fontaine) shape a people's comic sense; lack of such traditions can lead to grotesque national responses in controversy. Implication: study of comic masters cultivates the faculty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing comic interpretation from crude realism
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not know that the fly in amber is of any particular use, but the Comic idea enclosed in a comedy makes it more generally perceptible and portable... A very good, innocent young man is her victim, or a very astute, goodish young man obstructs her path... The triumph of a candid realism is to show him no hero.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realism that merely copies life (crude realism) can lack comic framing; enclosing a comic idea in an artistic scheme makes the comic clearer and more portable. Anti-pattern: presenting life as mere specimen without guiding comic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding farce when the Comic spirit is required
rubrics_metrics.description: The Comic spirit eyes but does not touch it. Put into action, it would be farcical. It is too gross for Comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farce and gross buffoonery may produce laughter but not the intellectual, restrained laughter of true Comedy. Keep comic perception and presentation from descending into mere vulgarity or farce.
